title: The Shipwrecked Man and the Sea
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Shipwrecked Man cast up on the beach fell asleep after his struggle with the waves. When he woke up, he bitterly reproached the Sea for its treachery in enticing men with its smooth and smiling surface, and then, when they were well embarked, turning in fury upon them and sending both ship and sailors to destruction.

The Sea arose in the form of a woman, and replied, "Lay not the blame on me, O sailor, but on the Winds. By nature I am as calm and safe as the land itself: but the Winds fall upon me with their gusts and gales, and lash me into a fury that is not natural to me."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Shipwrecked Man do after his struggle with the waves?
options: He immediately searches for other survivors
He builds a fire to signal for help
He falls asleep on the beach
He begins swimming back out to sea

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the man do when he wakes up?
options: He bitterly reproaches the Sea for its treachery
He thanks the Sea for sparing his life
He asks a passing traveller where he is
He falls asleep again from exhaustion

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the man accuse the Sea of doing to sailors?
options: Refusing to let any ship pass safely at all
Warning sailors away before a storm arrives
Freezing over so suddenly that ships become trapped
Enticing them with a smooth surface, then turning on them in fury

questions.prompt: According to the passage, in what form does the Sea appear to answer the man?
options: As a great wave
As a woman
As an old sailor
As a seabird

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who does the Sea say is really to blame for the storms?
options: The sailors themselves
The moon and the tides
The Winds
The ships' captains

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Sea describe her own nature?
options: As calm and safe as the land itself
As unpredictable as the weather
As dangerous as any storm
As mysterious as the deepest night

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Sea say the Winds do to her?
options: They calm her whenever a storm begins
They avoid her entirely during the summer months
They ask her permission before a voyage begins
They fall upon her with gusts and gales, and lash her into a fury

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the man blame the Sea rather than the weather in general?
options: He does not believe the Winds have any real power
He experienced the Sea directly as the force that destroyed his ship
He was told by other sailors that the Sea alone was at fault
He has never heard of storms being caused by wind

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "treachery" mean in "reproached the Sea for its treachery"?
options: A show of great strength
A sudden change in weather
A betrayal of trust
A generous act of kindness

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: What appears to be the true cause of harm may really be driven by another, hidden force
The sea is always dangerous no matter how calm it looks
Sailors should never trust any body of water
Storms are entirely unpredictable and cannot be explained

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where does the man wash up after the shipwreck?
options: On a rocky cliff
On a small island
Near a fishing village
On the beach

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the man describe the Sea's surface before a storm?
options: Dark and churning
Smooth and smiling
Cold and grey
Loud and roaring

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the man say happens to ship and sailors once the Sea turns in fury?
options: They are guided safely to shore
They are delayed but ultimately saved
They are sent to destruction
They are warned in time to turn back

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the Sea's defense be considered a reasonable explanation rather than a mere excuse?
options: She describes a natural state disturbed by an outside force, rather than denying the danger occurred
She provides no explanation at all, only an apology
She proves that no storm has ever truly happened
She blames the sailors for sailing during bad weather

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the phrase "not natural to me" suggest about how the Sea views her stormy behavior?
options: It is something she deliberately chooses to do to sailors
It happens only once every few years by chance
It is a trait she shares equally with the Winds
It is an exception caused by outside forces, not her true character

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "embarked" mean in "when they were well embarked"?
options: Having returned safely to shore
Having boarded a ship and set out
Having repaired a damaged vessel
Having sold their cargo at port

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A shipwrecked man is rescued by a kind sea spirit
A shipwrecked man refuses to ever sail again after hearing the Sea's reply
A shipwrecked man blames the Sea for his misfortune, but she points instead to the Winds
A shipwrecked man argues that the Winds are blameless
